title: Circling the Garage
story: A camera at the entrance of a parking garage reads the plate of every car that drives in and writes it to a log, in order. A driver who finds no free spot leaves by the exit ramp and often comes straight back in to try again.
The manager wants to know if that happened: the same plate coming in twice within a few entries of itself. The same car returning hours later is a normal visit, not circling.
task: Write circlingCar(plates, k). Return true if there are two positions i < j with plates[i] === plates[j] and j - i ≤ k. Otherwise return false.
An empty log returns false. With k = 0 no pair can qualify, so the answer is false.

examples.explanation: Plate 77 came in at positions 1 and 3. 3 - 1 = 2, which is within k = 2, so the answer is true.
Plate 512 came in twice, at positions 0 and 4. 4 - 0 = 4 is more than k = 3, so that was a normal second visit. No other plate repeats. The answer is false.
Plate 8 came in at 0, 4 and 6. Comparing with its first visit gives gaps of 4 and 6, both too big. But visits 4 and 6 are only 2 apart, so the answer is true.

hints: In [3, 9, 3] with k = 2, the 3s are at positions 0 and 2. When you reach position 2, what single fact about plate 3 do you need from the past?
Only the most recent earlier visit of a plate matters. If that visit is too far back, every older visit is even further back.
Keep one number per plate: the position where you last saw it. Which structure gives you that number in one step?
Walk the log with a map from plate to last position. At each position j, if the plate is in the map and j - last ≤ k, return true. Either way, update the map to j. Return false at the end.
bruteForce: For each entry, compare it with the next k entries and return true on a match.
That costs about n × k comparisons. With 100,000 entries and k = 100,000 it is billions of checks. The waste is that every entry looks forward again over cars the earlier entries already looked at.

js: * @param {number[]} plates  plate numbers in entry order
* @param {number} k  the largest gap that still counts as circling
py: def circling_car(plates: list[int], k: int) -> bool:

tests.note: a repeat exists but too far apart: defeats plain duplicate checks
only the latest visit is close: defeats keeping the first position

js: const last = new Map(); // plate -> position of its latest entry
if (last.has(plates[j]) && j - last.get(plates[j]) <= k) return true;
last.set(plates[j], j); // this is now the latest visit
py: last = {}  # plate -> position of its latest entry
if plate in last and j - last[plate] <= k:
last[plate] = j  # this is now the latest visit
walkthrough: This is the duplicate check from Double-Scanned Tickets with a distance limit. A set is no longer enough, because you need to know where you last saw a plate. So store the position.
• Positions 0 to 3: plates 8, 1, 2, 3 are all new. Map: 8 → 0, 1 → 1, 2 → 2, 3 → 3.
• Position 4, plate 8. Last seen at 0, gap 4 > 2. Not circling. Update 8 → 4.
• Position 6, plate 8. Last seen at 4, gap 2 ≤ 2. Return true.
The update in step 2 is the important line. If you kept the first position, 8 → 0, the last visit would see a gap of 6 and you would wrongly answer false.
solution.timeWhy: One pass, and each map lookup or update is O(1) on average.
solution.spaceWhy: With no repeats the map ends up holding every plate. Keeping only the last k plates in a set would cut this to O(k).
solution.takeaway: When a match only counts if it is close enough, store the latest position of each value in a hash map instead of just whether you saw it. The most recent occurrence is always the best candidate.
